own_scenes.desc: El new wave, que escondía una docena de variantes (punk, synth-pop, nuevos románticos, gótico, ska…), llegó al Medio Oeste vía Chicago y prendió entre el público negro de Detroit como en ningún otro sitio: los primeros discos electrónicos de la ciudad reconcilian a Human League, los B-52’s o Visage con el eurodisco, el funk de Clinton, Zapp y Ohio Players y el soul de Motown. Los preps adoraban los grupos de estética pulida; de Visage gustaba más que «Fade to Grey» su cara B instrumental, «Frequency 7». La Yellow Magic Orchestra fue un Kraftwerk más juguetón, y su «Technopolis» anticipa a Cybotron; ABC, Heaven 17 y Human League, desde la Sheffield siderúrgica, ofrecían una sofisticación fingida (Penthouse and Pavement, The Luxury Gap) que copiaron los clubes de instituto. Es la «doble refracción» de Jon Savage: los grupos europeos que idolatraban eran a su vez reflejo de la música negra americana.

influences.name: Eurodisco e italo-disco: el «progressive» de Detroit

refs.q: Just as Italo-disco had, new wave caught on with African American audiences in Detroit like nowhere else in the United States.
refs.para: Just as Italo-disco had, new wave caught on with African American audiences in Detroit like nowhere else in the United States. One could hear new wave’s offbeat and eclectic ingredients working themselves out in Detroit’s early electronic dance records, where groups like the Human League, the B-52’s, and Visage were reconciled with Eurodisco, the Midwestern funk of George Clinton, Zapp, the Ohio Players, and, subconsciously, the soul of Motown. Detroit’s preps connected with the style-conscious synth-pop bands, which had exterior styles as well polished as their sound; a subset of synth-pop—the “new romantics”—even bordered on foppish, such as the group Visage. “Fade to Grey” was Visage’s biggest hit, but it was the flip side that captured the Motor City’s attention. Simply titled “Frequency 7,” it was a surprisingly aggressive and swaggering instrumental, especially considering the new romantics’ predilection for dramatic vocals and delicate melodies. Perhaps it was the influence of former Magazine member and future Bad Seed Barry Adamson that pushed their sound in this direction.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Party Out of Bounds: The Pre-History of Techno, 1978–1983

refs.q: By the same token, while it may seem strange that Detroit’s African American teenagers were listening to the angular, almost robotic disco and soul from Europe, the European groups they idolized were themselves reflections of American music.
refs.para: This is where author Jon Savage’s notion of “double refraction” becomes essential to understanding the sometimes nonlinear evolution of dance music. “Double refraction” refers to the process by which music is passed and copied back and forth between cultures. In his book England’s Dreaming: Anarchy, Sex Pistols, Punk Rock and Beyond, Savage writes of England’s pub bands in the 1970s: “Most of these groups were copying white British pop groups—like the Rolling Stones or the Yardbirds—that were themselves trying to capture the spirit of black American R&B.” By the same token, while it may seem strange that Detroit’s African American teenagers were listening to the angular, almost robotic disco and soul from Europe, the European groups they idolized were themselves reflections of American music.

notes.chapter: Cap. 8: Fundido en gris: el pop vampirizado por la electrónica en los ochenta (1977-1989)
notes.text: Acercar la electrónica al pueblo con canciones pop pegadizas. The Human League (Sheffield, 1977) es el primer grupo pop inglés en las listas con un sonido frío y electrónico; Heaven 17 su escisión. El sello ZTT de Trevor Horn (Buggles, Frankie Goes to Hollywood, Propaganda, Art of Noise) y la factoría Stock, Aitken & Waterman convierten el synth-pop en éxito masivo; Bronski Beat y Soft Cell, en reivindicación gay. Depeche Mode, «synth-pop con actitud» (Mute, con Daniel Miller como «casi un padre»), OMD, Yazoo/Erasure de Vince Clarke y Pet Shop Boys, quizá la mejor banda pop eléctrica de la década. En Bélgica, Telex; en Suiza, Yello.

notes.chapter: Cap. 21: Apéndice 2 · El salto cuántico: avances exponenciales en la tecnología musical (1836-2017)
notes.text: Fairlight CMI (1979) y Synclavier abren la era digital del sampler; el MIDI (1982, Kakehashi, Dave Smith y Tom Oberheim) conecta todas las máquinas; el Yamaha DX7 (1983) y su síntesis FM definen el sonido de los ochenta.

refs.q: un joven cuarteto de Manchester llamado New Order
refs.para: Quizá su carácter profético y prometeico quede plenamente demostrado por el hecho de que una vez la revolución tecnológica quedó consolidada, su papel tendió a ser menos necesario y su figura se vio superada en lo musical por aquellos a los que habían servido de inspiración. Pese a que la edición del portentoso maxi «Tour de France» (EMI, 1983) —homenaje al deporte favorito de Ralf, ciclista prácticamente compulsivo— les confirmó su buena forma, bloquearon a ultimísima hora la publicación de Technopop. Y es que por esas fechas un joven cuarteto de Manchester llamado New Order publicaba un par de maxis titulados «Blue Monday» y «Confusión» (el segundo producido por Arthur Baker), que amedrentaban a cualquiera. Con la excusa de actualizar el sonido y los equipos que debían producirlo en Kling Klang, el proyecto se retrasó hasta Electric Cafe (EMI, 1986), avanzado en lo visual gracias a Rebecca Allen, pero mucho más flojo en lo musical. Pese a que se puede volver a escuchar con cariño, no tiene cabida en su etapa dorada, y anticipó ese mutismo paranoico de nuestros días en el que The Mix (EMI, 1991), recopilatorio de autoversiones modernizadas, es poco más que una excusa para una gira restringida que pasó por el festival británico Tribal Gathering, donde varias generaciones de artistas y ravers les dieron una calurosa acogida y, ya en 1992, por un macroconcierto antinuclear organizado por Greenpeace y U2 frente a la planta nuclear de Selkfield (Inglaterra), ciudad que habían incluido en la nueva versión de un «Radioactivity» abiertamente antinuclear, en el que la frase «it’s…

refs.q: la cuna del primer grupo pop inglés que consiguió entrar en las listas de ventas con un sonido frío y electrónico
refs.para: Sheffield fue un punto clave, y no precisamente por ser sede de un enjambre de bandas adscritas de una manera u otra a la escena industrial (Cabaret Voltaire, Clock DVA, Huía), sino por ser la cuna del primer grupo pop inglés que consiguió entrar en las listas de ventas con un sonido frío y electrónico: The Human League. La contraportada de Travelogue (1980) recogía un lema que describía sus intenciones: «contains synthesizers + votáis only», algo completamente acorde con la influencia recibida (Kraftwerk, por supuesto) y sus intenciones del todo rompedoras. Fundada por Martyn Ware e Ian Marsh —que habían formado parte de los grupos Dead Daughters y Future— en 1977, The Human League se completó con la entrada del vocalista Philip Oakey, y sus primeros pasos en el sello punk Fast contrastaron con el furor guitarrero de sus coetáneos: Reproduction (1979) era un tejido de sintes y tonos mecánicos (como el ruido generado por máquinas de vapor), uno de los pocos discos de pop fuera del ámbito Kraftwerk que podrían considerarse adelantados a su tiempo, exactamente lo mismo que el citado Travelogue, un estudio de la textura y el tono electrónico que merece rescatarse.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: Fundido en gris: el pop vampirizado por la electrónica en los ochenta (1977-1989)

refs.para: Afortunadamente, durante los ochenta no todas las discográficas dedicadas al synth-pop tenían una política de promoción y control tan agresiva como ZTT o SAW por lo que los resultados, si bien no tan espectaculares en un primer momento, sí eran mucho más memorables (sobre todo desde el enfoque artístico) a largo plazo. Sin lugar a dudas en ese ámbito hay pocas bandas nacidas en los ochenta que puedan competir con Depeche Mode. También synth-pop, sí, pero «con actitud». «Depeche Mode eran una banda de pop con electrónica, un tipo de pop nuevo... no eran una boy band porque no fue una banda manufacturada, sino que todo surgió de una manera muy natural», recuerda Daniel Mller, miembro en la sombra de los de Basildon —fue su ingeniero de sonido en los primeros discos— y algo más que el propietario del sello para ellos («Mller fue fundamental durante los diez primeros años: productor, asesor, casi un padre», declaró Andrew Fletcher a Rockdelux en 1997). No hay, pues, sospechas de dirigismo, lo que les permitió sembrar y recoger en una carrera creciente desde Speak and Spell (Mute, 1981) («sus influencias eran el punk, Kraftwerk, claro, los primeros singles de The Human League y el glam de Roxy Music. No tenían las influencias de los sesenta, sino las de los setenta») hasta Music for the Masses (Mute, 1987), que no debe nada al cliché afeminado de los nuevos románticos. «A los fans de Spandau Ballet o Steve Strange no les gustaba Depeche Mode. Depeche era una banda cien por cien electrónica a la que no le interesaba el rock camuflado de Duran Duran. Estaban más cerca de…

refs.q: si hay en los ochenta alguna banda de pop eléctrico que pueda superar a Depeche Mode, esa es sin duda Pet Shop Boys
refs.para: …con cierta tendencia al mesianismo (que Dave Gahan siempre ha interpretado a la perfección) que quizá se haya hecho más patente en sus imitadores. «Cuanto mejores son las canciones, más futurista te permiten ser. New Order también venían de la sensibilidad post-punk, y aunque al principio no eran electrónicos, supieron cómo manejar sus instrumentos para conseguir una fuerza similar. Pet Shop Boys venían de otro lugar, eran más kitsch, más disco. Neil Tennant había sido un periodista musical, y sabía lo que se hacía: todos sus movimientos eran bastante calculados. Depeche surgió de una manera más espontánea, y New Order salían de su propio interior. No eran bandas cool que hacían manifiestos.» Se acepta el codazo de Daniel Miller a Pet Shop Boys por venir de quien viene, pero que conste que si hay en los ochenta alguna banda de pop eléctrico que pueda superar a Depeche Mode, esa es sin duda Pet Shop…

refs.q: Y aquí es donde hace aparición el MIDI (1982)
refs.para: Y aquí es donde hace aparición el MIDI (1982), un protocolo creado por Ikutaro Kakehashi, Dave Smith y Tom Oberheim que, con la intención de jubilar los anteriores métodos —el DIN Sync (1980) diseñado por Kakehashi, que no tenía en cuenta ciertas complejidades en los nuevos sistemas electrónicos—, permite que los instrumentos electrónicos, ordenadores y otros dispositivos habilitados con puertos de entrada y salida MIDI se comuniquen entre sí. Esto le da la capacidad al usuario para manejar el tono y la intensidad de la nota, señales como la dinámica o el vibrato, y hasta lanzar una claqueta capaz de sincronizar el tempo entre los distintos dispositivos. Todos los mensajes se envían mediante uno o varios cables MIDI a los demás instrumentos, controlando así cualquiera de los parámetros necesarios para la generación de sonidos u otras características. El lenguaje era tan perfecto —hay que reconocer la genialidad a sus tres creadores— que a duras penas ha cambiado desde el día de su creación. Es más: la penúltima revolución musical de los últimos cuarenta años aparece con la entrada del MIDI y sus avanzados métodos de interconexión a los nuevos samplers y sintetizadores digitales, como los dos modelos de Ensoniq, el ESQ-1 (1986) y el SQ-80 (1988), primeros en demostrar que la nueva revolución digital también contaba con los bolsillos más humildes. Sería también el año en que llegaría la MPC60 (1988), brillante y ambiciosa idea de Roger Linn, producida por la marca japonesa Akai, que unía la capacidad de muestrear sonidos externos a un potentísimo secuenciador y dieciséis…

refs.q: La síntesis FM fue uno de los avances más destacados de los años ochenta
refs.para: …la síntesis, como el PPG Wave (1981/1984) del ingeniero alemán Wolfgang Palm. En sus tres distintas versiones pudo renovarla por completo, aplicando un nuevo concepto llamado tabla de ondas o wavetable, en el que distintas muestras microscópicas se repetían hasta crear una señal constante. Los diferentes sonidos se podían retocar luego gracias a los distintos filtros, envolventes ADSR y demás valores, dando a pie a miles de combinaciones distintas. Por las mismas fechas llegó el Yamaha DX7 (1983), sintetizador digital que, en tiempo récord, volvió a darle la vuelta a la tortilla creando un nuevo tipo de síntesis: consistía en variar la frecuencia de una señal (portadora) con respecto a una segunda (moduladora), generando finalmente una onda modulada en frecuencia o de frecuencia modulada. La síntesis FM fue uno de los avances más destacados de los años ochenta. A pesar de que programar el DX7 era un verdadero infierno —había que manejarse a través de su delirante submenú solo con unos incómodos botones de membrana, un potenciómetro y una pequeña pantalla LCD—, los complejísimos sonidos que podía crear definieron la música de casi cualquier banda de la época, de las mas renombradas —Talking Heads, Jan Hammer, A-Ha, Enya, The Cure, Depeche Mode—, a las más desconocidas. Desde percusiones metálicas a bajos de textura analógica, pero fríos como una piedra, pasando por cuerdas y vientos sacados de los más húmedos sueños de neón. No solo marcó su época, sino que está considerado el segundo sintetizador más vendido de la historia (más de ciento sesenta mil unidades) después del…

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Influence (late 1976)
podcast.body: In late 1976, Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren was quoted in *Melody Maker* magazine using the term "new wave." He applied it to bands that, though related to punk and sharing its essence, did not necessarily sound strictly punk, helping the term gain traction within a year to describe underground music emerging from punk. "Later that year, late 76, a story in Melody Maker magazine quoted Sex Pistols Manager Malcolm McLaren, very artsy guy. And he was using the term and applying it to bands that were related to punk, part of the same seamst punk, but not necessarily sounding that punk at all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of the Term (1976)
podcast.body: The earliest known references to the phrase "New Wave" appeared in the British fanzine *Sniffing Glue* in 1976. The writers intended to draw a connection between the lofty artistic ambitions of British punks and the "renegade French filmmakers of the 50s and 60s" who pioneered the French Nouvelle Vague movement. "The earliest references we can find to that phrase are in a British fanzine called Sniffing Glue in 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defining Characteristics (UK, 1977-78)
podcast.body: The first era of British New Wave (around 1977-78) was described as spiky, angular, and somewhat agitated, representing a shift from aggressive punk to a more existential despair ("from being about F you to we're F'd"). Some bands were also upbeat and fun, characterized by sharp suits, skinny ties, and choppy, sharp-sounding power pop with clever or geeky lyrics. "One of the best descriptions I've ever read about this era of British music is that things went from being about F you to we're F'd."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Emergence in 1977
podcast.body: The year 1977 is considered the beginning of New Wave, alongside punk rock and post-punk, marking a significant shift in music after the earlier prolific years of rock. "1977 punk, the beginning of New Wave, the era of post punk and all that came with it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence in 1977
podcast.body: The term "New Wave" began to be heard in 1977, marking a new development in music. "It's also the year when we began to hear of something called New Wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Usage (1977)
podcast.body: By the late 1970s, Malcolm McLaren, a former manager of The New York Dolls, began using the term to describe "cool new bands that weren't quite punk," leading to interchangeable use of "punk" and "new wave" by the end of 1977. "Malcolm McLaren, a one-time manager of the New York dolls, started throwing at the term when he was trying to describe cool new bands that weren't quite punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: North American Acceptance (1977)
podcast.body: By the end of 1977, the term "New Wave" gained traction in North America, with mainstream publications like *Time* and *Newsweek* covering the "punk slash New Wave movement," despite initial confusion over its exact definition. "By the end of 1977, the phrase had caught on in North America. Time and Newsweek, which is about as mainstream as you can get, both wrote stories on the punk slash New Wave movement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Sire Records Marketing Campaign (Early 1977)
podcast.body: Sire Records, led by Seymour Stein, launched a marketing campaign in early 1977 called "Don't Call it Punk" to re-brand British punk rock that was evolving into something more melodic, less violent, and less political. They aimed to "blunt the negative perceptions" associated with punk by heavily promoting "New Wave" as a replacement term for "punk" and "underground." "And so in early 1977, Sire launched a marketing campaign called Don't Call it Punk and began leaning heavily on the term New Wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: 1978 Emergence and Characteristics
podcast.body: New Wave began to appear in 1978 as punk was peaking and burning out. It resulted from a cross-pollination between punk's attitude and pop's melody, featuring twitchy, spiky, choppy, and nervous sounds with experimental structures, geeky vocals, artsy intellectualism, and a suburban vibe, contrasting with traditional rock's blues roots. "Pop and punk had a baby, and they called it New Wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution, including the emergence of synth-pop (referred to as "signpok" and associated with synthesizer music). "nacían el signpok"

podcast.title: 1978-1984 Era and Evolution
podcast.body: The New Wave scene, roughly from 1978 to 1984, can be divided into two periods. The first saw a proliferation of guitar-driven alternative pop bands, liberated by punk to experiment and emerging from cities beyond New York and London, such as Toronto, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Akron, Ohio. "And as these new groups started to come to our attention, many of them came from cities other than New York and London, the two main centers of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: North American Phenomenon (1978-1984)
podcast.body: The New Wave era predominantly manifested as a North American phenomenon, spanning from approximately 1978 to 1984. This period was characterized by two distinct phases, with the first featuring hundreds of guitar-driven pop bands inspired by 1960s British and American rock, and liberated from conventional thinking by the influence of punk. "Stepping back just a little, we can see that the new wave era became mainly a North American phenomenon that stretched from 1978 through to about 1984."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, concurrent with the ongoing Post-Punk scene, New Wave music was emerging. This period was characterized by a rapid birth and diversification of musical styles. "en 1979, estaban naciendo la vez el new wave."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Era (1979-1985)
podcast.body: The New Wave era began in 1979 and maintained a strong presence until at least 1985. It transitioned from an underground sound connected to punk rock to becoming a very mainstream genre, defining the mainstream for a period. "The New Wave era started in 1979 and had a good run before it was done by, oh at least 1985."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Malcolm McLaren's Early Advocacy (Late 1979)
podcast.body: Starting in late 1979, art-oriented members of the British punk community, notably former Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren, attempted to popularize the phrase "New Wave." McLaren sought to use this term to describe the musical landscape in the months following the Sex Pistols' breakup. "The art C1s amongst the British punk community, including ex-sextal manager Malcolm McLaren, tried to get people to accept this word, this phrase beginning in late 1979, as Malcolm sought to describe his world in the months after the sex pistols broke out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: US Breakthrough Summer (1979)
podcast.body: The summer of 1979 was the definitive "breakthrough summer of New Wave" in America, marked by power pop bands like Cheap Trick, The Knack, and The Cars achieving their highest-charting hits. "In America, that was the breakthrough summer of New Wave, as power pop bands like Cheap Trick."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Major Label Adoption (By 1980)
podcast.body: Seymour Stein's "New Wave" marketing term was swiftly embraced by major labels, including Warner Brothers Records and Polygram Records. By 1980, this led to "New Wave" becoming a widely used catch-all term for a broad spectrum of experimental, artsy, and more poppy music that emerged in the wake of punk. "Seymour's marketing term was then picked up by Warner Brothers Records, and then by Polygram Records, and then other major labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strong Presence in New York (1980)
podcast.body: New Wave was a very potent musical force in New York around 1980, exemplified by bands like Devo. "El New Wave en Nueva York. Allá en 1908 entra a muy potente, gracias adivo, entre otras bandas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack Introduction (1980)
podcast.body: The soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square* was one of the very first to feature the nascent new wave and punk rock music of the day. Despite the movie and double LP's dismal sales, for those who purchased it, it offered an immediate look at cutting-edge music and significantly contributed to introducing people to these genres. "Time Square did a lot to introduce people to punk a new wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Pilot (1981)
podcast.body: Gary Numan, a prominent figure in the new wave music scene, was not only an influential musician but also an accomplished pilot. In 1981, he successfully completed a flight around the world in his own aircraft, showcasing a remarkable adventurous spirit beyond his musical career. "Gary Newman, the new wave star, turned electronic icon to guys like Back in Dave Grohl, became very accomplished as a pilot, even working as a stunt pilot in air shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: A "Different Wave" in 1982
podcast.body: In 1982, artists like Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello, Graham Parker, and Nick Lowe were charting a "different wave" of New Wave that defied confinement to traditional rock, pop, jazz, or soul categories, distinct from the prevailing synth pop and MTV-driven New Wave of the era. "Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello, Graham Parker and their peer, Nick Lowe were charting a different wave. One that couldn't be confined to rock, pop, jazz or soul."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Peak Popularity and MTV Influence (1982-1983)
podcast.body: New Wave experienced its peak popularity in 1982 and 1983, a period significantly bolstered by the debut of MTV in 1981 and MuchMusic in 1983. These music video channels provided a new visual platform for music, turning "telegenic New Wave bands" like Flock of Seagulls, Eurythmics, and Duran Duran into major stars. "New Wave was at its biggest through 1982 and 1983. The music video certainly helped too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1983 Musical Landscape
podcast.body: In 1983, one of the two dominant musical camps for musicians was "synthesizers with dance beats," representing a style that The Smiths deliberately eschewed. The Smiths' success is credited with hastening the decline of this genre. "or B, you were into synthesizers with dance beats."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: Second British Invasion Impact (1983-1984)
podcast.body: Starting in 1982 and 1983, British New Wave bands, along with New Romantic groups, transitioned from "curios" to "video superstars" and "chart conquerors" in America by 1984. Fuelled by MTV, these movements, exemplified by acts like Duran Duran and Eurythmics, "redefined the cutting edge of cool" in the US. "The bands that had benefited the most from the rise of the music video in America were British New Romantic and New Wave bands, who, starting in 1982 and 83, went from Curios in America to Viva."

podcast.title: Bond Theme Strategic Shift (1985-1987)
podcast.body: Following the success of Duran Duran's "A View to a Kill" in 1985, James Bond producers strategically decided that the "new wave sound was definitely the way to go" for future themes. This led to A-Ha being hired for "The Living Daylights" in 1987, aiming to attract new audiences to the somewhat stale franchise. "The producers decided that the new wave sound was definitely the way to go."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Madonna's New Wave Interpretation (1985)

"After the nihilism of punk and all of this talk about burning down the past and rebuilding the present, people were actually ready for something new."

podcast.body: In contrast to post-punk, New Wave was generally characterized by a less dark or gloomy sensibility and possessed significantly greater commercial potential. It served as an expansive umbrella term for a variety of subgenres, including Power Pop (e.g., Elvis Costello, Tom Petty), the 2 Tone scene (e.g., The Specials, English Beat), and Technopop (bands favoring synthesizers over guitars). podcast.title: Chronological Span and Sub-periods
podcast.body: The New Wave era generally extended from approximately 1978 to 1984. This period can be further divided into two main phases: an initial phase characterized by jerky, twitchy, fun power pop often based on guitars, bass, and drums, and a later, synthesizer-driven phase known as Technopop. "Now the new wave era extended roughly from 1978 through to about 1984. And we can divide that span into two periods."

podcast.title: Rapid Mutation and Decline (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: The New Romantics scene mutated quickly, with fashion evolving from outrageous to sharp suits. Despite peripheral associations with groups like Ultravox, Japan, and Adam Ant, the rapid changes led to the scene largely burning out by 1982. "The New Romantic scene mutated rapidly. Fashion moved from the outrageous to sharp suits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reaction to 70s Rock
podcast.body: By the late 1970s, a new sound called New Wave emerged, pushing back against the prevailing trend of 70s rock, which had become characterized by long songs, big solos, and a perception that everything had to be "super important." Early New Wave, exemplified by songs like Nick Lowe's "Cruel to Be Kind," focused on being tight, catchy, and concise (under three minutes). It was about "getting in, saying something and then you get out," prioritizing efficiency over grandiosity. This genre allowed radio listeners and casual fans to engage with something new that was not overly difficult to understand, bridging the gap between punk and classic 70s rock. "New wave especially the early version of it pushes back on this idea and Cruel to be kind is a perfect example of how to do that."

podcast.title: Reading Festival Adoption
podcast.body: The Reading festival was one of the first major festivals to embrace British new wave music, alongside British punk and British metal. "It also became the first major festival to really embrace British punk and British new wave as well as British metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rebellion Against Disco
podcast.body: New Wave developed, in part, as a rebellion against what was perceived as the "hideousness of disco." It offered an alternative musical space for fans seeking sounds different from the polarizing offspring of R&B. "Freed from the rigid dogma of punk and anxious to rebellion to the hideousness of disco, the subgenres just kept on coming."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Recurring Application for New Movements
podcast.body: Despite its evolving definition, the term "New Wave" has persistently been used to describe new waves of music in later periods. Examples include the new wave of modern psychedelia (Tame Impala) and the rock revival (The Strokes, The White Stripes, Interpol, Bloc Party). "fue una palabra que se quedó ahí un tanto atascada pero que regularmente incluso más adelante hemos seguido usando cada vez que venían nuevas oleadas de música."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Resurgence as "Disco in Another Guise"
podcast.body: By 1982 and 1983, as New Wave synth pop began emerging on the charts, its sound was "essentially disco in another guys." This modernized pop style, exemplified by ABC's "The Look of Love," helped to bring dance-oriented music back into the mainstream without using the "dirty word" disco. "But by 1982 and 83 as New Wave synth pop began emerging on the charts, the sound of this so-called new pop was essentially disco in another guys."

podcast.body: The experimental nature of early San Francisco punk, with its eclectic blend of styles, helped set the stage for the development of new wave music. "The result was some very interesting experimentation, which set the stage for later rock, new wave, and technopop sounds."

podcast.title: Second Wave and Synthesizers (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: The second wave of New Wave began around 1980 with the widespread adoption of synthesizers, which became cheaper, more portable, and powerful. Musicians, often without formal training, experimented with synths to create new and futuristic sounds, leading to the birth of synth-pop. "The second wave began in earnest in about 1980 with the widespread introduction of synthesizers."

podcast.title: Separation from Punk in the US
podcast.body: Similar to the UK, the US scene, particularly at CBGB, featured both pure punk bands like Ramones and non-punk bands like Talking Heads and Blondie. Over time, "punk" became associated with Ramones-style music, and bands that didn't fit this mold were categorized as New Wave. "poco a poco en Estados Unidos se le fue perdiendo el miedo a la parada a punk y se fue quedando el punk ya para la generación de los ramones y de la gente que hacía esas versiones, lo que conocemos en el punk. Y el resto de bandas que no encajaban dentro de esa nueva enclatura eran los que estaban considerados en New Wave."

podcast.title: Seymour Stein's Marketing Strategy
podcast.body: Seymour Stein, the founder of Sire Records, strategically adopted "New Wave" as a marketing term to sell his artists' records in America. This was in response to radio stations' apprehension about playing "punk" records, which they perceived as too weird, violent, political, or merely a fad. Stein used "New Wave" to "disguise things and soften the blow," making the music more palatable for mainstream radio. "That's when Seymour started using the phrase New Wave to market his stuff. It was a way to disguise things and soften the blow."

podcast.body: Following its initial use for mainstream rock, "New Wave" quickly became associated with alternative and underground movements. podcast.body: Facing resistance to "punk rock" on mainstream radio, Sire Records, led by Seymour Stein, launched a "Don't Call It Punk, Call It New Wave" campaign around Christmas 1976. This marketing rebrand successfully removed the stigma, making the music more palatable for radio and the public. "So Sire launched a NAD campaign called Don't Call It Punk, urging people to call this new music New Wave."

podcast.title: Slickness Through Technology
podcast.body: New Wave's distinct "slick" sound was partly due to advancements in music technology, specifically the development of more powerful and polyphonic synthesizers, as well as expensive sampling devices like the Fairlight CMI. "And it was also very slick, thanks to some new technological inventions."

podcast.body: New Wave music was cost-effective to license for movie soundtracks, a factor exploited by director John Hughes for films like *Sixteen Candles*, *Pretty in Pink*, and *The Breakfast Club*, filling their albums with edgy, new bands, many from the UK. podcast.title: Subgenres and Decline (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: New Wave became a broad category, leading to the emergence of subgenres like synthpop (including New Romantics), dark guitar-focused bands (Public Image Limited, Joy Division, The Cure), "dorky" bands (Devo, B-52s, Oingo Bongo), and post-disco new wave (New Order, Dead or Alive, Eurythmics, The Human League). Some acts, like Culture Club and Wham!, stripped away punk DNA. By 1985, the concept of New Wave became too unwieldy and meaningless due to blurring genre differences, leading to its decline. "by 1985, the genre differences were just too blurry in all the commonalities had been wiped out."

podcast.body: In the 1980s, new wave artists demonstrated a remarkable ability to take obscure songs, such as B-sides or deep album cuts, and transform them into major chart successes, exemplified by Soft Cell's "Tainted Love" and Kim Carnes' "Bette Davis Eyes." podcast.title: Trent Reznor's Early Aspiration
podcast.body: Trent Reznor was profoundly inspired by synth-pop bands like The Human League, OMD, and Depeche Mode, finding their synthesizers and drum machines "really cool," to the extent that he once considered a job working for a company that made them. podcast.title: Two Versions Merge (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: By the end of the 1970s, there were distinct UK and American versions of New Wave, characterized as an energetic, guitar-based, slightly jittery brand of power pop, often featuring musicians in suit jackets and skinny ties. "By the end of the 70s, there were two slightly different versions of New Wave, one for America and one for the UK."

podcast.body: The band 999 is identified as a punky new wave act from the UK, known for their 1978 track "Homside." "It's a 1978 track from a punky new way back from the UK called 999."

podcast.title: UK Scene and Clubs (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: The New Romantics scene emerged in the UK in the late 1970s, centered around clubs in London, Birmingham, and Liverpool, such as the Blitz Club, Billies, and Erics. This movement was marked by its distinctive fashion and musical styles. "a new scene called New Romantics took hold in a few clubs in London, Birmingham, and Liverpool in the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK vs. US Terminology in Late 70s
podcast.body: In the United Kingdom, the term "punk" was initially avoided due to its negative, violent, and anti-establishment connotations, especially linked to anarcho-political movements. Thus, "New Wave" differentiated non-punk underground movements from punk. In the United States, "New Wave" continued to be used almost interchangeably with "punk" for several years. "en el reino nido se diferenciaba el punk, de lo que era el punk del new wave, era lo que todo el movimiento underground, que no era el punk, en Estados Unidos todavía eran reacios, y se seguía usando el new wave casi como sinónimo de punk durante muchos años."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Undefined Nature
podcast.body: New Wave is cited as an example of a musical movement for which no one has been able to provide a clear definition, as it encompassed many similar but not identical elements, similar to the debate around shoegaze and dreampop. "no aun nadie consigue dar una definición clara de que era el new wave porque cumula muchas cosas parecidas que no eran exactamente iguales."

podcast.title: Visual Emphasis and Image
podcast.body: New Wave was significantly influenced by MTV, as the channel's existence made visual appearance a critical factor in an artist's success. Marketers and directors began to emphasize "looks and glitz," often leading to style surpassing substance, with New Wave bands being particularly well-suited to this visual medium. "MTV quickly began to affect the course of music because it began to really matter what you looked like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Expression Controversy
podcast.body: New Wavers were among the artists whose new forms of vocal expression, facilitated by microphones, generated decades of strong criticism from purists. Their singing styles were considered by some to be "degenerate forms of singing," challenging the established vocal norms of earlier generations. "R&B acts, Elvis, The Beatles, Dylan, Jagger, New Waivers, rappers all the way up to and beyond death medillars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Style Development
podcast.body: As New Wave gained popularity, new vocal styles began to emerge, with singers often sounding "geeky" and unashamed. This reflected a musical ethos that was catchy, fun, and perceived as more authentic than mainstream offerings, providing artists a license to be silly and goofy in a fashionable and artistic manner. "Singer sounded, uh, kind of geeky, orn't ashamed of it, because they didn't care."
